source_text: Nec uerbis tantum sed et factis Deus orare nos docuit ipse orans frequenter et deprecans et quid nos facere oporteret exempli sui contestatione demonstrans, sicut scriptum est: ipse autem fuit secedens in solitudines et adorans, et iterum: exiuit in montem orare et fuit pernoctans in orationem Dei. quodsi ille orabat qui sine peccato erat, quanto magis peccatores oportet orare, et si ille per totam noctem iugiter uigilans continuis precibus orabat, quanto nos magis in frequentanda oratione debemus nocte uigilare!
thought_title: Prayer by example, not only by words
orientation: Cyprian is showing that the Lord taught prayer not only by his words but by his own practice of praying, and he now applies that example to sinners.
pass_a_gloss: Not by words only but also by deeds God to pray us he taught [him]self praying frequently and beseeching and what us to do it behoved [by] example of his own [by] witness showing, as it is written: [he] himself but was withdrawing into desert places and praying, and again: he went out into [the] mountain to pray and was passing [the] night in prayer [to] God. But if he was praying who without sin was, how much more sinners it behoves to pray, and if he through [the] whole night continually keeping watch [with] unbroken prayers was praying, how much [more] we in frequenting prayer ought [by] night to keep watch!

choices.english: by the testimony of his example
choices.why: Keeps the legal-witness force of contestatio, which Cyprian uses to mean a public proof or attestation, not a mere illustration.
rejected: by the proof of his example

choices.why: Solitudines is plural and concrete; 'lonely places' preserves the plural and the sense of deserted spots, not an abstract solitude.

choices.english: he was spending the night in prayer to God
choices.why: The periphrastic fuit plus present participle is a literal rendering of the Old Latin idiom, and 'prayer to God' keeps the directional in plus accusative.
rejected: he spent the night in prayer to God
he continued all night in prayer to God

choices.english: continually keeping watch with unbroken prayers
choices.why: Iugiter and continuis both stress unceasingness; rendering both preserves Cyprian's emphatic doubling.
rejected: keeping vigil all night with ceaseless prayers

choices.why: The gerundive frequentanda has an active, repeated-practice sense; 'frequenting prayer' keeps the verbal force rather than turning it into an adjective.

bible_refs.note: ipse autem fuit secedens in solitudines et adorans
exiuit in montem orare et fuit pernoctans in orationem Dei

pass_b_english: God taught us to pray not only with words but also with deeds, praying and pleading often himself, and showing us by the testimony of his example what we ought to do. As it is written: “He himself was withdrawing into lonely places and praying” (Luke 5:16), and again: “He went out to the mountain to pray, and he was spending the night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12). If he who was without sin prayed, how much more ought sinners to pray! And if he kept watch through the whole night, continually praying with unbroken prayers, how much more ought we to keep watch at night in frequenting prayer!

last_rejected.source_quote: ipse autem fuit secedens in solitudines et adorans
last_rejected.why: The verse cited is Luke 5:16, but this matches Luke's wording poorly; Mark 1:35 or a synoptic parallel is closer, and the Latin follows an Old Latin tradition not well-identified as Luke 5:16.
last_rejected.fix: Luke 5:16 [or as some manuscripts have it]
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'secedens in solitudines' matches Luke 5:16 Old Latin; citation is defensible, not a major error.

last_rejected.source_quote: exiuit in montem orare et fuit pernoctans in orationem Dei
last_rejected.why: The verse cited is Luke 6:12, but the Latin reads 'orationem Dei' (prayer to God), while Luke 6:12 has 'proseuche tou theou' or similar; the citation should be checked against the Old Latin tradition.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'pernoctans in orationem Dei' matches Luke 6:12 Old Latin tradition; citation is defensible, not wrong.
